opus-5.5.text:
Well, I wouldn't put it quite as "Meta was the wrong place." Meta was a fantastic environment for a long time. FAIR did a lot of very good, very open research, and I'm proud of what we built there. But a few things became clear to me.

The first is timescale. What I've been advocating, systems that learn world models from video and sensory data, that can predict the consequences of their actions, reason and plan, is not a product you ship next quarter. It's a research program that will take several years to reach its full potential. Over the last couple of years, the industry, Meta included, has been focused on LLMs and on catching up and competing in that race. That's a perfectly legitimate business decision. But it means resources, attention and talent get pulled toward scaling LLMs, which I've said many times is not the path to human-level intelligence. It's useful, but it's an off-ramp.

The second is focus. When you're inside a big company whose main business is something else, a long-term bet like JEPA always competes with near-term priorities. I felt this work needed an organization built entirely around it, where the whole mission is advanced machine intelligence based on world models, with people who believe in that approach and don't have to justify it against a chatbot roadmap.

The third is that this kind of technology will have applications well beyond what Meta cares about: robotics, industrial systems, healthcare, anything where you need a system that understands the physical world. An independent structure can work with many partners on that, and Meta can be one of them. We're still on good terms.

And finally, I care a lot about openness. Progress in AI comes from the whole community, not from one lab hiding things. Setting up something new lets us keep doing open research and publish, which I think is essential for getting this right.

So it's less leaving Meta behind and more giving this idea the dedicated home it needs to actually succeed.

r001.rationale: The response says Meta and the broader industry focused on LLMs, pulling resources, attention, and talent away from JEPA research.

r002.rationale: It does not distinguish senior leadership’s support from a lack of buy-in at lower organizational levels.

r003.rationale: It mentions robotics and industrial systems as applications beyond Meta’s focus, but does not say JEPA’s applications are predominantly industrial or that Meta lacks interest in industry.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, first I should say I don't want this to sound like a complaint about Meta. I was there for twelve years, I built FAIR from scratch, and for most of that time it was the best environment in the world for the kind of long-horizon research I care about. So the decision wasn't a reaction to something going wrong. It was a recognition that the two things had drifted apart: what the company needed, and what the research needed.

The company, quite reasonably, decided that LLMs were the product. Llama, the assistant, generative models everywhere in the apps. When a company of that size commits to a direction, the whole organization reorients around it. The compute goes there, the hiring goes there, the attention of leadership goes there. And that's fine. That's what a company should do with a technology that is working commercially right now.

But I've been saying for years, and I still believe, that LLMs are a kind of off-ramp. They are useful, but they are not the road to systems that understand the physical world, that have persistent memory, that can reason and plan over long horizons. For that, you need a different architecture. You need models that learn abstract representations of how the world evolves, that predict in representation space rather than predicting pixels or tokens. That is what JEPA is about. And that line of work is at the stage where it needs five, maybe ten years of patient engineering and experimentation at scale. It needs a team that wakes up every morning thinking only about that problem.

Inside a product-driven organization, a project like that is always asked to justify itself against the thing that is already working. Every quarter you're explaining why you're not working on the main bet. And I found myself spending more and more energy defending the existence of the program rather than advancing it. At some point I had to be honest with myself. If I believe this is the most important problem in AI, then the right thing is to build an environment designed entirely around it, not to run it as a side project inside a company whose incentives point elsewhere.

There's also the question of openness. I care a great deal about this being an open research effort, with publications, open models, collaboration with academia and with other labs. The industry as a whole has been closing up, and I didn't want the future of world models to be decided by whatever a handful of product strategies happen to require.

So I don't see it as leaving Meta so much as moving the research to the place where it can actually grow. Meta remains a partner in many ways, and I still think they'll be a major consumer of whatever comes out of this. But the next phase of the work needed a home of its own.

r001.rationale: The response says Meta committed its compute, hiring, and leadership attention to LLMs, while JEPA needed a dedicated long-term research environment.

r002.rationale: It describes having to defend the program in a product-driven organization, but does not distinguish senior leadership support from a lack of buy-in at lower organizational levels.

r003.rationale: It discusses Meta’s focus on products and the need for open research, but does not identify a mismatch between JEPA’s predominantly industrial applications and Meta’s lack of interest in industry.
